content:
The shortlisted wineries and wine tourism businesses have been revealed for the 2027 Best Of Wine Tourism Awards in South Australia.

Presented as part of Adelaide’s membership in the Great Wine Capitals Global Network, the Best Of Wine Tourism Awards “recognise innovation and excellence in a sector that continues to play a major role in attracting visitors to South Australia”.

The awards aim to celebrate the diversity of South Australia’s wine tourism industry across seven categories: ‘Accommodation’, ‘Architecture and Landscape’, ‘Art and Culture’, ‘Culinary Experiences’, ‘Innovative Wine Tourism Experiences’, ‘Wine Tourism Services’ and ‘Sustainable Wine Tourism Practices’.

This year, 11 outstanding wineries and wine tourism operators have been shortlisted, with winners to be announced at the SA Wine Industry Dinner on Thursday 17 September at the National Wine Centre.

The 2027 shortlisted businesses are:

  • Beresford Estate, McLaren Vale
  • BK Wines, Adelaide Hills
  • Chateau Tanunda, Barossa
  • d’Arenberg, McLaren Vale
  • Home of Plenty, Currency Creek
  • Jacob’s Creek, Barossa
  • National Wine Centre, Adelaide
  • On Cockatoo Lane, Barossa
  • Paulett Wines & Bush deVine Restaurant, Clare Valley
  • Slate Restaurant at Pikes Wines, Clare Valley
  • Tscharke Wines, Barossa

Claire Scriven, Minister for Primary Industries and Regional Development, congratulated the finalists.

“South Australia is recognised around the world for our premium wine and outstanding visitor experiences, which are underpinned by hard work, innovation and passion for our wine industry.

“The Best Of Wine Tourism Awards are a celebration of the exceptional people and businesses that showcase the best of South Australia and make a valuable contribution to our regional communities and economy,” she said.

Winners will be chosen by an independent panel featuring “prominent South Australian wine and tourism leader Helen Edwards AM, renowned wine journalist Katie Spain and Adelaide University associate professor and marketing scientist Justin Cohen”.

The businesses who win the awards will go on to compete in the international Best Of Wine Tourism Awards, presented during the Great Wine Capitals Global Network’s annual conference in Hawke’s Bay this October, where they will be benchmarked against other leading wine regions from around the world.

Minister for Tourism Emily Bourke said it is great to see wine tourism operators and producers from so many regions making the shortlist.

“Our wine regions are among the state’s most sought-after visitor destinations, offering world-class experiences that showcase the best of South Australia.

“These awards celebrate the passion, creativity and commitment of the people who help make our regions such special places to visit, and I congratulate the operators who have made the shortlist for these prestigious industry accolades,” Bourke said.

Each South Australian winner “will also be profiled throughout the year for their significant contributions to the state’s wine tourism sector”.

The awards are presented in partnership with DrinkWise, an independent, not-for-profit organisation that promotes responsible alcohol consumption.

Six wineries from across the Mudgee region of NSW will come together on Saturday 12 September at 6pm for ‘The Sustainable Table’, an evening of wine, food and conversation about the future of Australian wine.

Presented by the Mudgee Wine Association as part of the Mudgee Wine & Food Festival 2026, the long-table dinner will showcase six Sustainable Winegrowing Australia member or certified member wineries, including Bunnamagoo, Logan, Rosby, De Beaurepaire, Yeates and Steins.

Held at Logan Wines, guests will be served a three-course seasonal menu by Olive.A.Twist, paired with wines from the participating wineries.

The Sustainable Table aims to put a human face to sustainability, “connecting people with the growers and makers shaping the future of Mudgee wine”.

“We created The Sustainable Table to shine a light on the winemakers and vignerons already working towards more sustainable winegrowing and to showcase the innovation happening across our region. It’s an opportunity to share what sustainability looks like in practice and the different ways Mudgee wineries are thinking about the future,” said Sarah Yeates of the Mudgee Wine Association.

The participating wineries will share the real-world ways they’re growing grapes more sustainably – from improving soil and managing water to protecting biodiversity, regenerating vineyards and adapting to a changing climate.

“We’re thrilled to see sustainably minded producers collaborate to deliver this inspiring event, an experience that celebrates exceptional local produce and wines, while also shining a spotlight on the passionate individuals and sustainability stories behind every bottle and harvest,” said Siobhan Wigan, executive officer of Sustainable Winegrowing Australia.

Alepat Taylor has announced its appointment as the exclusive Victorian distributor for Down the Rabbit Hole winery in McLaren Vale.

The appointment comes at an “exciting time” for Down the Rabbit Hole, following its recent recognition at the Halliday Wine Companion 2027 Awards where it won the People’s Choice Award.

For Alepat Taylor, the appointment represents “an opportunity to bring a highly differentiated South Australian wine brand to Victorian retailers, restaurants, bars and wine lovers”.

“We are extremely excited to be appointed as the Victorian distributor for Down the Rabbit Hole. It is a brand that has all the ingredients we look for, quality wine, a strong point of difference, an authentic story and an exceptional connection with consumers,” said Jimmy Lekkas of Alepat Taylor.

“The recognition from Halliday is a fantastic endorsement of the experience that Domenic, Elise and the team have created at McLaren Vale. It demonstrates that Down the Rabbit Hole is much more than a wine brand, it is a destination and an experience that people genuinely connect with.

“We see a significant opportunity to introduce the brand to more Victorian consumers and trade customers and to build on the success Down the Rabbit Hole has already achieved in South Australia.”

The partnership will see Alepat Taylor focus on developing Down the Rabbit Hole across the Victorian market, with a “targeted approach to independent retailers, leading restaurants, wine bars, hospitality groups and other on-premise venues”.

Domenic and Elise Palumbo, founders of Down the Rabbit Hole, said they are thrilled to bring their wines to Victoria.

“We’ve always wanted Down the Rabbit Hole to be about more than what is inside the bottle. It’s about bringing people together, enjoying great wine and food, and creating memories. Alepat Taylor shares that passion for brands with personality and purpose, and we’re really excited about what we can achieve together in Victoria.”

House of Cards also received two gold medals for its 2025 Royals Chardonnay (98 points) and 2024 Kings in the Corner Cabernet Merlot (95 points). Moreover, the winery was awarded the ‘IWSC Trophy for Western Australian Producer of the Year’, marking the second time the winery has received this prestigious trophy, following its first win in 2024.

content:
House of Cards has made history with its 2025 Ace High Chardonnay. Image credit Bianca Kate Photography

Margaret River winery House of Cards has made international wine history with its 2025 Ace High Chardonnay awarded the first ever 100-point score at the 2026 International Wine & Spirit Competition (IWSC) Global Tasting in Margaret River.

The accolade also makes the 2025 Ace High Chardonnay the highest-scoring wine ever awarded by the IWSC, following “rigorous blind judging by some of the world’s leading wine judges and Masters of Wine”.

House of Cards also received two gold medals for its 2025 Royals Chardonnay (98 points) and 2024 Kings in the Corner Cabernet Merlot (95 points).

Moreover, the winery was awarded the ‘IWSC Trophy for Western Australian Producer of the Year’, marking the second time the winery has received this prestigious trophy, following its first win in 2024.

IWSC co-chair of judges Freddy Bulmer, wine buyer for The Wine Society in the UK, said the 2025 Ace High Chardonnay stood out for its sheer class, depth, complexity and perfect balance.

“When Andrew Caillard MW, who was co-chairing with me, suggested 100 points, I thought: there’s nothing more that this wine could do. We tasted it again, blind, alongside all the gold medal wines at the end of the judging, and both agreed that 100 points was absolutely justified. It was an absolutely beautiful wine — absolute perfection,” Bulmer said.

Owners Travis and Liz Wray said they were thrilled by the results, particularly the recognition achieved through blind judging.

“We are absolutely blown away that our wines have been so successful after being blind-judged by some of the world’s best judges and MWs,” they said.

“To be tasted next to other world-class wines and being awarded a perfect 100 points is something dreams are made of.

“The Margaret River wine region is consistently producing world-class wines and we are so proud that our wine has produced the first-ever perfect 100-point score.”

Only 1,300 bottles of the 2025 Ace High Chardonnay were produced.

The Margaret River continued to see success at the competition when Annabel Angland, viticulturalist at Cape Mentelle, was awarded the inaugural ‘IWSC Young Wine Producer Award’. Open to those aged 35 or under who had direct responsibility for winemaking or viticulture, the trophy is based on the aggregate points achieved by their wines, which included a gold for Cape Mentelle’s Heritage Chardonnay 2025.

A total of 29 gold medals were awarded, with the top three wines all Margaret River Chardonnay. Presenting the gold medals at the IWSC Awards Sundowner, Andrew Caillard MW praised the unmistakable character and world-class quality of Margaret River Chardonnay, highlighting the powerful expression of the Gingin clone.

“How magnificent the Gingin clone is here, how unique, how wonderful it is and how diverse it is… this commonality and voice that is so clear cut, I really found it extraordinary.

“This year, it was really crystal clear you have got something really unique and special,” Calliard said.

This year’s Margaret River judging panel brought together leading international and Australian wine voices, led by Co-Chairs Andrew Caillard MW and Freddy Bulmer, alongside UK-based judges Emma Robinson, Isa Bal MS and Joanna Nerantzi, and Australian judges Nick Ryan, Kayleen Reynolds and Loïc Avril.

The IWSC judging panel in Margaret River. Image supplied

Over the week, the IWSC judges were immersed in the Margaret River Wine Region, gaining first-hand insight into the land, culture, people and wines that have helped shape Western Australia’s global wine reputation. Christelle Guibert, IWSC Strategy and business development director, highlighted the importance of spending time in the region for the judges.

“What always stands out in Margaret River is the passion and generosity of its producers. Spending time with them throughout the week gives our international judges a much deeper understanding of the region – not only the quality of the wines, but the people, vineyards and stories behind them.”

The wines were judged blind at the Vasse Felix Art Gallery from 26–28 August, with more than 250 entries assessed through the IWSC’s rigorous judging process across key varieties including Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz and Sauvignon Blanc.

Margaret River Wine Association CEO Penny Dickeson said hosting one of the world’s most respected international wine competitions in the region created value well beyond the official judging.

“Bringing influential judges to Margaret River is an investment in more than medals. It puts our producers in direct conversation with global trade, media and sommeliers, creating relationships, market insight and advocacy that continue long after judging has finished.”

content:
Every bottle from Witches Falls Winery reflects careful work at every stage of production. Behind the scenes, LPG, carbon dioxide and nitrogen support essential winery processes, from moving product around the site to packaging and purging, helping keep operations running reliably from start to finish.

“Winemakers want to make wine, they don’t want to talk about gas.”

For Keelan Standen, Field Sales Manager QLD at Supagas, the line captures what good gas supply should look like in a working winery.

At Witches Falls Winery on Tamborine Mountain, the finished bottle is only the visible end point of a much broader process.

Across the site, product and materials need to be moved, packaging needs to be supported and the wine itself needs to be handled with care. Behind those activities sits a collection of practical inputs that rarely take centre stage but still need to work as expected.

Gas is one of them.

Witches Falls uses LPG for forklifts to move products around the site. Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is used in packaging and purging; nitrogen is also used for purging.

Each gas has a different role, but together they form part of the day-to-day rhythm that allows the winery team to keep its attention on the product.

Supporting the work behind the wine

For Winemaker Abby Heslop, one of the main benefits of the relationship with Supagas is simple: the gas is there when they need it.

“What I appreciate most about dealing with Supagas is they’re always reliable, they’re consistent,” Abby says. “We’re able to get gas weekly, so our production isn’t held up.”

That reliability matters across very different parts of the operation.

The LPG used in forklifts helps keep things moving, allowing product and materials to be shifted where they are needed, when they are needed.

CO₂ and nitrogen come closer to the winemaking process itself. Both are used in purging applications, while CO₂ also supports packaging.

For Abby, that places particular importance on gas quality.

“With the CO₂ and the nitrogen, it’s in direct contact with the product,” she says. “So we want to make sure it’s as high quality as possible.”

Confidence in the quality of those gases matters because of the care already invested in the wine. Attention to the product does not stop once the winemaking is done; it carries through the processes that help prepare it for the finished bottle.

A working winery on Tamborine Mountain

Tamborine Mountain is an important part of the winery’s setting, although Keelan says it can sometimes be considered out of the way from a servicing perspective.

For Witches Falls, that makes having a supplier able to work reliably within the location especially valuable.

“Historically, Supagas has worked with our ‘Yes We Can’ approach to make sure we get gas on time to the customers, no matter where they are in the delivery footprint,” Keelan says.

When that support works as intended, it largely disappears into the background. Forklifts keep moving, packaging can continue and purging can happen when required, without the winemaking team having to spend unnecessary time managing another supply issue.

That matters commercially as well as operationally.

A delay in one supporting input can quickly flow into the wider production schedule. For a winery, keeping product moving through packaging, handling and dispatch means protecting productive time and avoiding interruptions that can add cost or delay finished wine getting where it needs to go.

Reliable gas supply therefore has a practical business value: it helps keep the operation moving and allows the people responsible for the wine to stay focused on the work that creates value.

Quality and continuity behind the scenes

For Witches Falls, the relationship with Supagas began with reliable support when it mattered most. According to Keelan, maintaining that standard has remained the priority.

“The relationship with Witches Falls started back in 2013, based on our ability to service in a timely fashion,” he says. “Our job is to maintain that level of service and keep it seamless.”

From LPG through to the CO₂ and nitrogen used around the product, gas supports several parts of the winery without needing to become a major focus for the team.

That is perhaps the clearest measure of whether the relationship is working.

Much of what keeps a winery productive sits behind the finished bottle. Some of it requires constant attention from the winemaker. Other parts should simply work when required.

Gas supply falls into that second category.

When the right gases are available when needed, the winery can keep materials moving, maintain its production schedule and reduce the risk of avoidable interruptions. In practical terms, that means less time spent solving supply problems and more time spent producing and moving wine.

Keelan puts it most simply.

“Winemakers want to make wine, they don’t want to talk about gas. Our role is to provide the gas seamlessly, so they can focus on their work.”

At Witches Falls, that means production behind the bottle can keep moving while the focus stays where it belongs: on the wine.

content:
Wineries are invited to get involved with the returning Fiano Festa campaign, which will run through spring and summer to introduce new customers to the varietal ahead of Fiano Day on 16 October 2026.

According to Mastermind Consulting and Oliver’s Taranga Vineyards in McLaren Vale, last year’s campaign found “widespread success in both reach and product sales”.

The total reach for 2025 was approximately 2.7 million with 24.5 thousand social media interactions, 350 non-social media mentions and a 58% increase in Google searches for Fiano wine.

“We were thrilled to see a significant uplift in Fiano sales across all channels,” said Corrina Wright, director at Oliver’s Taranga Vineyards.

“We attribute this success to the groundswell created by the Fiano Festa campaign, and the variety’s ability to convert white wine drinkers into ongoing Fiano fanatics.”

Mastermind Consulting said waves were felt across the entire industry, with producers Australia-wide reporting increased demand from consumer, retail and on-premise outlets.

“Fiano has resonated with consumers for many reasons, particularly its suitability for enjoying with so many different cuisines,” said Trish Barry, CEO at Mastermind Consulting.

“Trends in white wine suggest customers are looking for easy-drinking, aromatic wines, and Fiano is exactly that.”

Last year’s campaign provided downloadable assets for wineries to utilise and the phrase ‘Fiano Fridays’ was leveraged as a social media hook to share the message.

“The campaign was not prescriptive; wineries and venues could get on board at a level that worked for them. The key was simplicity and explaining the wine style in context, noting that for many consumers, this was a new discovery,” said Barry.

Erin Leggat, CEO of McLaren Vale Wine Region, shared that the region “has become the home of premium Fiano in Australia”.

“It is extremely well suited to both our coastal Mediterranean climate, and our relaxed beachside lifestyle. Fiano offers wine lovers an exciting new way to experience McLaren Vale,” Leggat said.

However, Wright added that Fiano Festa has always been bigger than just one winery or region.

“Seeing producers, retailers and consumers embrace the variety so enthusiastically was incredibly rewarding. Our own Fiano sales uplift was a fantastic result, but the real success was bringing the regions together to shine a spotlight on Australian Fiano and create opportunities for everyone producing this exciting variety.”

Unico Zelo, which sells a range of Fianos spanning the Riverland, Adelaide Hills and Clare Valley, noted seeing a noticeable impact from the collective Fiano Festa campaign.

“Last year’s Festa was the first time strangers walked into our cellar door and asked for Fiano by name. We’d been shouting about this grape on our own for over a decade and never got that. One month of shouting together did it,” shared Brendan Carter of Unico Zelo.

Wendy Laureti from Hunter Valley’s Saddlers Creek Wines also observed a “very positive outcome” from last year’s Fiano Festa.

“Our Fiano sales almost doubled over the months of September and October last year. Being part of national conversation gave a small Hunter Valley Fiano a sense of scale it couldn’t earn on its own.”

In the Barossa, James Lienert, winemaker at Lienert Vineyards, saw the “excellent adaptation Fiano had to the vineyards in McLaren Vale”.

“We thought that it could work out in the Western Barossa, at the very least it was worth having a go.

“We bottled the wine around October 2025 with 1500 litres, which sold out in approximately 3.5 months, far surpassing our expectations of 6 to 12 months. As a result, we more than tripled production. If the trend continues, we will look to increase the production again next year,” Lienert said.

Fiano Festa is an open-invitation campaign, with more information available from Mastermind Consulting and Oliver’s Taranga Vineyards.

“Collaboration over competition was definitely a part of the Fiano Festa campaign’s success and we can’t wait to do it all over again,” finished Barry.

title: Rochford Wines owner passes Toolangi brand and assets to chief winemaker
summary:
Helmut Konecsny, owner of Yarra Valley-based winery Rochford Wines, has passed the winery’s Toolangi brand and vineyard assets to his long-serving winemaker, Kaspar Hermann, as well as his family, “ensuring Toolangi remains a family-owned vineyard as it becomes independent”. Toolangi now operates independently under Hermann’s direction and with Rochford’s full support. Hermann will continue his role as winemaker for both houses. “Wine is made by people, not portfolios,” Konecsny said. “Kaspar has poured his heart into these wines. He has walked these rows through frost and heatwave, through hard vintages and great ones. A winery is not barrels and buildings – it is the people who give their lives to it. The proudest thing an owner can do is not to hold on, it is to hand over – well, to the right hands. Toolangi is in the right hands.” For Hermann, the transition “fulfills a lifelong dream and a winemaker’s oldest ambition: a family name behind the family’s wines”.

Toolangi now operates independently under Hermann’s direction and with Rochford’s full support. Hermann will continue his role as winemaker for both houses.

“Wine is made by people, not portfolios,” Konecsny said.

“Kaspar has poured his heart into these wines. He has walked these rows through frost and heatwave, through hard vintages and great ones. A winery is not barrels and buildings – it is the people who give their lives to it. The proudest thing an owner can do is not to hold on, it is to hand over – well, to the right hands. Toolangi is in the right hands.”

For Hermann, the transition “fulfills a lifelong dream and a winemaker’s oldest ambition: a family name behind the family’s wines”.

“Every winemaker carries a quiet dream that one day the wines they make might carry their own family’s name behind them,” Hermann said.

“Helmut has made that dream real for us. Nothing changes in the glass. The same vineyards, the same standards, the same hands on every vintage. What changes is the heart behind the label. My children will grow up knowing their name is on a vineyard, and that is because one man chose loyalty over consolidation.”

Rochford Wines said the move “keeps Toolangi in family hands in a region that has been losing family wineries, and extends the tradition the Yarra Valley was built on: families passing wine into the hands of families”.

Toolangi wines remain available through the Rochford cellar door and through continued distribution via its partners.

“We are backing our winemaking without reservation. Our goal is for Rochford to stand in the top tier of Australian wine, and Kaspar’s leadership across both houses is central to that,” said Konecsny.

By Hans Mick

The recently announced departures of two senior figures from major Australian wine organisations have raised concerns about the loss of experienced leadership and industry knowledge at a time of prolonged pressure on the sector.

Murray Valley Winegrowers chair Chris Dent said the announcements that Australian Grape & Wine CEO Lee McLean will leave at the end of September and Australian Wine Research Institute managing director Dr Mark Krstic will step down at the end of the year reflected the prolonged challenges facing the industry.

“These resignations don’t happen in isolation – they’re a symptom of the pressure this industry has been under for years.

“There are many very good people across the sector who have dedicated years to it, and we’re increasingly seeing experienced, capable people leave as a consequence of the prolonged downturn. That’s a real concern for the future,” Dent said.

“Being an industry leader in the current environment is incredibly challenging. The pressures on businesses, growers and industry organisations are enormous, and much of what’s driving it is well beyond any one leader’s control.

“It’s understandable that people get frustrated and fatigued after this long, or that they see better opportunities elsewhere in a more positive environment.”

Dent also acknowledged the contribution of both departing executives.

“I’d also congratulate both Lee McLean and Mark Krstic for their exemplary service and commitment to the wine industry. My concern is that we risk continuing to lose not only businesses and vineyards, but also the experience, knowledge and capability built across the industry over many years.

“Retaining good people and building the next generation of leaders has to be a priority — the industry can’t afford to keep losing this much experience.”

Asked about concerns over the loss of experienced leadership, Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said the government recognises the difficulties confronting the grape and wine sector.

“We know that the Australian grape and wine sector is facing a number of challenges, including global oversupply and changing consumer preferences, which is why we continue to work closely with the sector.

“While leadership decisions are ultimately a matter for individual organisations, strong industry organisations and research institutions have an important role to play in supporting the sector, advocating for its interests and helping it adapt to changing conditions.

“The Albanese Labor Government remains focused on supporting the sector’s long-term viability through market access, research and innovation, and practical reforms that help build a more sustainable future for Australian grape growers and winemakers,” the Minister said.

Riverina Winegrape Growers CEO Jeremy Cass also described the timing of the resignations as a surprise and reflected on the difficult circumstances in which both leaders had been operating.

“Both the resignations of Lee McLean, CEO of Australian Grape & Wine, and Mark Krstic, MD of AWRI, came as a surprise when the news dropped recently, especially since they were so close together,” Cass said.

“Both have left their mark on the Australian wine industry which has been at its worst in living memory for the past five years.

“I feel especially for Lee who I know has tried to advocate the dire state of the industry only for this to fall on deaf ears as far as the Federal Government has been concerned. His task has been completely unrewarding with a huge amount of pressure from industry for government assistance and no real support.

“I wish them both well in their future endeavours and believe that they will still try to have a positive impact on the wine industry when the opportunities arise.”

The second year of the Australia-China Winemaker Immersion Program exchange to China is officially underway, following an opening ceremony event held on Friday at the Penfolds Magill Estate.

Designed to “foster deeper engagement between the Australian and Chinese wine industries and develop emerging winemaking and viticultural talent in both countries”, the Australia-China Winemaker Immersion Program is delivered in partnership between the Australian and Chinese wine industry associations – Australian Grape & Wine and the China Alcoholic Drinks Association – supported by government, industry and academic institutions across both countries, including Wine Australia, Treasury Wine Estates and the Wines & Spirits division of Chinese agricultural and food company COFCO.

“Since the first Penfolds wine was exported from South Australia to Shanghai in 1893, Treasury Wine Estates has continued to develop our business in the Chinese market. This program is an important part of our commitment to China by advancing shared industry capability through technical knowledge and expertise exchange,” said Kerrin Petty, chief supply & sustainability officer for Treasury Wine Estates.

Attended by industry colleagues, program partners and government representatives from Australia and China, including Acting Consul-General of the Consulate-General of the People’s Republic of China in Adelaide, Wang Hongsun, and Federal Member for Sturt, Claire Clutterham MP, the opening ceremony was an opportunity to recognise the four successful participants, who flew to China on Saturday.

The participants include Harry Scanlon, owner, winemaker and viticulturist at Scanlon Wines in the Adelaide Hills; Leila Davis, co-founder and winemaker from Beechworth-based Foreign Friends; Holly Edson, travelling winemaker and front of house manager at Noosa’s Atelier Wine Bar; and Mike Lyons, Treasury Wine Estates assistant vineyard manager in the Barossa Valley.

The group will spend four weeks in China during harvest season, gaining hands-on experience in two of the country’s premier winemaking regions: Shandong and Ningxia.

Scanlon said they are looking forward to being immersed in all aspects of China’s wine industry, including learning how producers there are developing their own identities and styles.

“I also hope to come away with a deeper understanding of the people behind the industry and build relationships that can continue to strengthen the connection between Australian and Chinese wine,” Scanlon said.

Davis is interested in how China is tackling challenges similar to those faced by the wine industry in Australia such as extreme climates, frost, water scarcity and long-term vineyard resilience.

“I want to understand the techniques and mindset behind adaptations, from vineyard management through to winemaking decisions, and bring back practical techniques I can share with the Australian wine community with a particular focus on sustainability and future proofing,” Davis said.

Meanwhile, Edson would like to learn more about how Chinese wineries distribute and market their wines.

“Most of all, I am excited by the opportunity to meet and learn from Chinese winemakers, viticulturists and other wine professionals, while building meaningful connections and sharing knowledge and experiences within the industry.”

Lyons believes the program is an “incredible opportunity” to build relationships and exchange ideas.

“I am particularly keen to learn more about Chinese vineyard management practices, sustainability initiatives, climate adaptation strategies, and the approaches being used across China’s emerging wine regions.”

The program will include “practical immersions at leading Chinese wineries” including Penfolds Ningxia, Chateau Junding and COFCO Great Wall, academic exchange at China Agricultural University in Beijing and a visit to the China International Fair for Trade in Services, one of the country’s four major national trade fairs. The program will conclude on 23 September, with a special event commemorating 40 years of the sister province relationship between South Australia and Shandong.

“This program is about building the next generation of relationships between the Australian and Chinese wine sectors. We hope participants return with new ideas, stronger networks and a deeper understanding of each other’s wine regions, consumers and production practices,” said Lee McLean, chief executive of Australian Grape & Wine.

“Those connections will be invaluable as our industries work together to respond to shared challenges and opportunities, from sustainability and climate adaptation to engaging the next generation of wine consumers.”

Xingsan Huo, secretary general, wine branch for the China Alcoholic Drinks Association said they are delighted to welcome the participants to China.

“In March, Chinese winemakers visited Australia’s industry with a thirst for knowledge. Now, we’re honoured to connect Australian winemakers and viticulturists to a land equally rich in winemaking wisdom.

“Wine is the essence of terroir and a bond of friendship – this exchange will be an opportunity to share winemaking expertise, and importantly, build a strong dialogue between our cultures. Participants will experience the unique charm of China’s wine regions, marking a new beginning for collaboration between the wine industries in our two nations,” Huo said.

CEO of Wine Australia Dr Martin Cole added that international collaboration “plays an important role in building capability across the global wine community”.

“The Australia-China Winemaker Immersion Program gives participants the opportunity to learn from their counterparts in China, gain new perspectives and bring valuable insights back to Australia. Wine Australia congratulates this year’s cohort. We look forward to seeing the benefits of these experiences flow back to their businesses and the broader Australian grape and wine sector,” Cole said.

The second of two reciprocal legs in the 2026 program follows the success of the Australian leg of the program in March, which saw four Chinese wine industry professionals immersed in key South Australian production regions, including the Adelaide Hills, McLaren Vale and Barossa Valley, during vintage.

“By strengthening bilateral industry relationships and facilitating practical knowledge sharing, the Australia-China Winemaker Immersion Program aims to support emerging industry talent to collaborate on common challenges such as climate adaptation, market access and sustainability,” organisers said.

In June, a Treasury Wine Estates delegation joined the Australia China Business Council visit to Yaochi Xiye winery in Xinjiang, reconnecting with Kou Yaqin, one of the Chinese winemakers who took part in the Australian leg of the program earlier in 2026.

During her time in South Australia, Kou explored “region-specific viticulture challenges of irrigation and rootstock selection for warm and dry growing conditions”. After returning to Xinjiang, Kou has successfully modified vineyard irrigation, with a longer-term rootstock project underway through a new nursery block developed with the Grape Research Institute of the Shandong Academy of Agricultural Sciences.

Organisers claimed this follow-up visit “reinforced the program’s core purpose: growing the wine industry in both nations by sharing ideas, collaborating and building enduring relationships that continue to shape their regions and the broader industry long after the exchange ends”.

content:
House of Cards has made history with its 2025 Ace High Chardonnay. Image credit Bianca Kate Photography

Margaret River winery House of Cards has made international wine history with its 2025 Ace High Chardonnay awarded the first ever 100-point score at the 2026 International Wine & Spirit Competition (IWSC) Global Tasting in Margaret River.

The accolade also makes the 2025 Ace High Chardonnay the highest-scoring wine ever awarded by the IWSC, following “rigorous blind judging by some of the world’s leading wine judges and Masters of Wine”.

House of Cards also received two gold medals for its 2025 Royals Chardonnay (98 points) and 2024 Kings in the Corner Cabernet Merlot (95 points).

Moreover, the winery was awarded the ‘IWSC Trophy for Western Australian Producer of the Year’, marking the second time the winery has received this prestigious trophy, following its first win in 2024.

IWSC co-chair of judges Freddy Bulmer, wine buyer for The Wine Society in the UK, said the 2025 Ace High Chardonnay stood out for its sheer class, depth, complexity and perfect balance.

“When Andrew Caillard MW, who was co-chairing with me, suggested 100 points, I thought: there’s nothing more that this wine could do. We tasted it again, blind, alongside all the gold medal wines at the end of the judging, and both agreed that 100 points was absolutely justified. It was an absolutely beautiful wine — absolute perfection,” Bulmer said.

Owners Travis and Liz Wray said they were thrilled by the results, particularly the recognition achieved through blind judging.

“We are absolutely blown away that our wines have been so successful after being blind-judged by some of the world’s best judges and MWs,” they said.

“To be tasted next to other world-class wines and being awarded a perfect 100 points is something dreams are made of.

“The Margaret River wine region is consistently producing world-class wines and we are so proud that our wine has produced the first-ever perfect 100-point score.”

Only 1,300 bottles of the 2025 Ace High Chardonnay were produced.

The Margaret River continued to see success at the competition when Annabel Angland, viticulturalist at Cape Mentelle, was awarded the inaugural ‘IWSC Young Wine Producer Award’. Open to those aged 35 or under who had direct responsibility for winemaking or viticulture, the trophy is based on the aggregate points achieved by their wines, which included a gold for Cape Mentelle’s Heritage Chardonnay 2025.

A total of 29 gold medals were awarded, with the top three wines all Margaret River Chardonnay. Presenting the gold medals at the IWSC Awards Sundowner, Andrew Caillard MW praised the unmistakable character and world-class quality of Margaret River Chardonnay, highlighting the powerful expression of the Gingin clone.

“How magnificent the Gingin clone is here, how unique, how wonderful it is and how diverse it is… this commonality and voice that is so clear cut, I really found it extraordinary.

“This year, it was really crystal clear you have got something really unique and special,” Calliard said.

This year’s Margaret River judging panel brought together leading international and Australian wine voices, led by Co-Chairs Andrew Caillard MW and Freddy Bulmer, alongside UK-based judges Emma Robinson, Isa Bal MS and Joanna Nerantzi, and Australian judges Nick Ryan, Kayleen Reynolds and Loïc Avril.

The IWSC judging panel in Margaret River. Image supplied

Over the week, the IWSC judges were immersed in the Margaret River Wine Region, gaining first-hand insight into the land, culture, people and wines that have helped shape Western Australia’s global wine reputation. Christelle Guibert, IWSC Strategy and business development director, highlighted the importance of spending time in the region for the judges.

“What always stands out in Margaret River is the passion and generosity of its producers. Spending time with them throughout the week gives our international judges a much deeper understanding of the region – not only the quality of the wines, but the people, vineyards and stories behind them.”

The wines were judged blind at the Vasse Felix Art Gallery from 26–28 August, with more than 250 entries assessed through the IWSC’s rigorous judging process across key varieties including Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz and Sauvignon Blanc.

Margaret River Wine Association CEO Penny Dickeson said hosting one of the world’s most respected international wine competitions in the region created value well beyond the official judging.

“Bringing influential judges to Margaret River is an investment in more than medals. It puts our producers in direct conversation with global trade, media and sommeliers, creating relationships, market insight and advocacy that continue long after judging has finished.”

content:
Every bottle from Witches Falls Winery reflects careful work at every stage of production. Behind the scenes, LPG, carbon dioxide and nitrogen support essential winery processes, from moving product around the site to packaging and purging, helping keep operations running reliably from start to finish.

“Winemakers want to make wine, they don’t want to talk about gas.”

For Keelan Standen, Field Sales Manager QLD at Supagas, the line captures what good gas supply should look like in a working winery.

At Witches Falls Winery on Tamborine Mountain, the finished bottle is only the visible end point of a much broader process.

Across the site, product and materials need to be moved, packaging needs to be supported and the wine itself needs to be handled with care. Behind those activities sits a collection of practical inputs that rarely take centre stage but still need to work as expected.

Gas is one of them.

Witches Falls uses LPG for forklifts to move products around the site. Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is used in packaging and purging; nitrogen is also used for purging.

Each gas has a different role, but together they form part of the day-to-day rhythm that allows the winery team to keep its attention on the product.

Supporting the work behind the wine

For Winemaker Abby Heslop, one of the main benefits of the relationship with Supagas is simple: the gas is there when they need it.

“What I appreciate most about dealing with Supagas is they’re always reliable, they’re consistent,” Abby says. “We’re able to get gas weekly, so our production isn’t held up.”

That reliability matters across very different parts of the operation.

The LPG used in forklifts helps keep things moving, allowing product and materials to be shifted where they are needed, when they are needed.

CO₂ and nitrogen come closer to the winemaking process itself. Both are used in purging applications, while CO₂ also supports packaging.

For Abby, that places particular importance on gas quality.

“With the CO₂ and the nitrogen, it’s in direct contact with the product,” she says. “So we want to make sure it’s as high quality as possible.”

Confidence in the quality of those gases matters because of the care already invested in the wine. Attention to the product does not stop once the winemaking is done; it carries through the processes that help prepare it for the finished bottle.

A working winery on Tamborine Mountain

Tamborine Mountain is an important part of the winery’s setting, although Keelan says it can sometimes be considered out of the way from a servicing perspective.

For Witches Falls, that makes having a supplier able to work reliably within the location especially valuable.

“Historically, Supagas has worked with our ‘Yes We Can’ approach to make sure we get gas on time to the customers, no matter where they are in the delivery footprint,” Keelan says.

When that support works as intended, it largely disappears into the background. Forklifts keep moving, packaging can continue and purging can happen when required, without the winemaking team having to spend unnecessary time managing another supply issue.

That matters commercially as well as operationally.

A delay in one supporting input can quickly flow into the wider production schedule. For a winery, keeping product moving through packaging, handling and dispatch means protecting productive time and avoiding interruptions that can add cost or delay finished wine getting where it needs to go.

Reliable gas supply therefore has a practical business value: it helps keep the operation moving and allows the people responsible for the wine to stay focused on the work that creates value.

Quality and continuity behind the scenes

For Witches Falls, the relationship with Supagas began with reliable support when it mattered most. According to Keelan, maintaining that standard has remained the priority.

“The relationship with Witches Falls started back in 2013, based on our ability to service in a timely fashion,” he says. “Our job is to maintain that level of service and keep it seamless.”

From LPG through to the CO₂ and nitrogen used around the product, gas supports several parts of the winery without needing to become a major focus for the team.

That is perhaps the clearest measure of whether the relationship is working.

Much of what keeps a winery productive sits behind the finished bottle. Some of it requires constant attention from the winemaker. Other parts should simply work when required.

Gas supply falls into that second category.

When the right gases are available when needed, the winery can keep materials moving, maintain its production schedule and reduce the risk of avoidable interruptions. In practical terms, that means less time spent solving supply problems and more time spent producing and moving wine.

Keelan puts it most simply.

“Winemakers want to make wine, they don’t want to talk about gas. Our role is to provide the gas seamlessly, so they can focus on their work.”

At Witches Falls, that means production behind the bottle can keep moving while the focus stays where it belongs: on the wine.

content:
Wineries are invited to get involved with the returning Fiano Festa campaign, which will run through spring and summer to introduce new customers to the varietal ahead of Fiano Day on 16 October 2026.

According to Mastermind Consulting and Oliver’s Taranga Vineyards in McLaren Vale, last year’s campaign found “widespread success in both reach and product sales”.

The total reach for 2025 was approximately 2.7 million with 24.5 thousand social media interactions, 350 non-social media mentions and a 58% increase in Google searches for Fiano wine.

“We were thrilled to see a significant uplift in Fiano sales across all channels,” said Corrina Wright, director at Oliver’s Taranga Vineyards.

“We attribute this success to the groundswell created by the Fiano Festa campaign, and the variety’s ability to convert white wine drinkers into ongoing Fiano fanatics.”

Mastermind Consulting said waves were felt across the entire industry, with producers Australia-wide reporting increased demand from consumer, retail and on-premise outlets.

“Fiano has resonated with consumers for many reasons, particularly its suitability for enjoying with so many different cuisines,” said Trish Barry, CEO at Mastermind Consulting.

“Trends in white wine suggest customers are looking for easy-drinking, aromatic wines, and Fiano is exactly that.”

Last year’s campaign provided downloadable assets for wineries to utilise and the phrase ‘Fiano Fridays’ was leveraged as a social media hook to share the message.

“The campaign was not prescriptive; wineries and venues could get on board at a level that worked for them. The key was simplicity and explaining the wine style in context, noting that for many consumers, this was a new discovery,” said Barry.

Erin Leggat, CEO of McLaren Vale Wine Region, shared that the region “has become the home of premium Fiano in Australia”.

“It is extremely well suited to both our coastal Mediterranean climate, and our relaxed beachside lifestyle. Fiano offers wine lovers an exciting new way to experience McLaren Vale,” Leggat said.

However, Wright added that Fiano Festa has always been bigger than just one winery or region.

“Seeing producers, retailers and consumers embrace the variety so enthusiastically was incredibly rewarding. Our own Fiano sales uplift was a fantastic result, but the real success was bringing the regions together to shine a spotlight on Australian Fiano and create opportunities for everyone producing this exciting variety.”

Unico Zelo, which sells a range of Fianos spanning the Riverland, Adelaide Hills and Clare Valley, noted seeing a noticeable impact from the collective Fiano Festa campaign.

“Last year’s Festa was the first time strangers walked into our cellar door and asked for Fiano by name. We’d been shouting about this grape on our own for over a decade and never got that. One month of shouting together did it,” shared Brendan Carter of Unico Zelo.

Wendy Laureti from Hunter Valley’s Saddlers Creek Wines also observed a “very positive outcome” from last year’s Fiano Festa.

“Our Fiano sales almost doubled over the months of September and October last year. Being part of national conversation gave a small Hunter Valley Fiano a sense of scale it couldn’t earn on its own.”

In the Barossa, James Lienert, winemaker at Lienert Vineyards, saw the “excellent adaptation Fiano had to the vineyards in McLaren Vale”.

“We thought that it could work out in the Western Barossa, at the very least it was worth having a go.

“We bottled the wine around October 2025 with 1500 litres, which sold out in approximately 3.5 months, far surpassing our expectations of 6 to 12 months. As a result, we more than tripled production. If the trend continues, we will look to increase the production again next year,” Lienert said.

Fiano Festa is an open-invitation campaign, with more information available from Mastermind Consulting and Oliver’s Taranga Vineyards.

“Collaboration over competition was definitely a part of the Fiano Festa campaign’s success and we can’t wait to do it all over again,” finished Barry.

Helmut Konecsny, owner of Yarra Valley-based winery Rochford Wines, has passed the winery’s Toolangi brand and vineyard assets to his long-serving winemaker, Kaspar Hermann, as well as his family, “ensuring Toolangi remains a family-owned vineyard as it becomes independent”.

A winery is not barrels and buildings – it is the people who give their lives to it. The proudest thing an owner can do is not to hold on, it is to hand over – well, to the right hands. “Helmut has made that dream real for us. Nothing changes in the glass. The same vineyards, the same standards, the same hands on every vintage. What changes is the heart behind the label. Rochford Wines said the move “keeps Toolangi in family hands in a region that has been losing family wineries, and extends the tradition the Yarra Valley was built on: families passing wine into the hands of families”.

Toolangi wines remain available through the Rochford cellar door and through continued distribution via its partners.

“We are backing our winemaking without reservation. Our goal is for Rochford to stand in the top tier of Australian wine, and Kaspar’s leadership across both houses is central to that,” said Konecsny.
